rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Components 2 Setup 3 Gameplay Overview 4 On Your Turn 5 End of game 6 Scoring 7 Options 8 Player Preferences Components 1 Game Board (center of the table) with 1 Round Marker 1 Player Board per player : with 5 colored progress markers + 5 colored auction markers 1 Nazar Stone (starting player marker) displayed on player side panel when assigned to a player 29 Market Tiles (Day) - 4 randomly removed 29 Market Tiles (Night) - 4 randomly removed 18 Outposts tiles unlimited currencies cards (Pardaos, Ships, Contracts, Compasses) 30 Exploration Cards unlimited Goods tokens of 5 types/colors Coconut coir Turmeric Pepper Silk Dried fish Setup The game starts with the day phase : 25/29 market tiles randomly placed on the 5x5 grid of the main board; later for the night phase 25/29 other market tiles will be randomly placed on the grid. 1 Exploration Card is drawn by each player until one player draw an Elephant symbol and becomes the starting player with 5 money, the others with 10. Gameplay Overview A game of Goa is divided into day and night cycles, each of which consists of 4 rounds. After the day cycle, remove all tiles from the playing area and setup the night tiles on the instead. At the end of the night cycle, the game ends and the player with the most points is declared the winner. Each round consists of 3 successive steps : 1. Place Auction Markers 2. Tile Auctions 3. Actions On Your Turn Step 1. Place Auction Markers : Each player places an auction marker on the grid. The first player places an auction marker and the starting player token on an empty space. Then each player places an auction marker next to the previous marker if possible. Step 2. Tile Auctions : Each player, starting with the player after the one who auctioned that tile/token has 1 turn to decide if they want to overbid or pass the auction related to the spots. The first auction is to gain the starting player marker + 1 compass card. All others are to gain the tile under the auction marker. The last player in the sequence (the same one who placed their auction marker on that tile/token) has these choices: They may accept the highest bid. The player with that bid pays the player who auctioned the tile. They may take the tile for themselves. The player pays 1 less than the highest bid to the supply. If no one bid anything, they may take the tile for free. Step 3. Actions : each player must play 1 possible action + max 1 card from their hand + play tiles from their hand until everyone played 3 actions. Then continue with players with compass cards (each action will cost 1 compass card), players cannot keep more than 1 compass card after this step (for future rounds). Basic actions are described as tooltips on player board column headers. In each case, the exact number of resources gained depends on how far you've progressed on that column. Progress : improve another basic action by moving down 1 of your own progress markers. Pay the listed number of trade goods and 1 ship for each good paid. Build Ships: collect ships from the supply. Produce goods: collect goods from the supply. You may only take goods if you have a depot that can store that good. Collect Taxes: collect money from the supply. Explore: draw Exploration cards. Unless otherwise specified, these can now be used for their effect at any time during your turn and do not consume an action (but can't be used for establishing an outpost anymore). After drawing, discard down to your hand limit. Establish an Outpost: attempt to collect an outpost tile. First, decide which tile you want. Then reveal two Exploration cards from the deck to see how many contracts you have (this is shown on the bottom left of the card). If those, the number of contracts from your progress marker, and the number of contract cards you're willing to spend add up to the number of contracts needed to establish that outpost, take the tile. Otherwise, take one contract card as a consolation prize. Cards actions are described in tooltips and help button (?) in the bottom left of the game Tiles actions are described in tooltips and help button (?) in the bottom left of the game End of game The game ends after 8 rounds (4 Day rounds + 4 Night rounds), then the game computes scores. Scoring You don't score anything during the game, but instead count different elements at the end : Progress Markers : Each of your Progress Markers scores between 0 and 10 points as indicated on the left of your Player Board row Outposts : You score between 1 and 10 points for your established Outposts : Number of Established Outposts Points 1 1 2 3 3 6 4 10 Island Symbols : Score Victory Points for each set of identical Island symbols shown on the Exploration Cards still in your hand ( Tiger / Elephant / Urn / Statue / Palm tree / Shell): Each symbol type scores between 1 and 15 points, depending on how many matching symbols you collected : Number of identical Island Symbols Points 1 1 2 3 3 6 4 10 5 15 Richest player : The player with the most money scores 3 points Tiles : Each tile with a specified score gives you those points, but if you also have the Foreman tile, you score 3 points instead of 1 for single-field Depots Be careful with the Duty tile (see page 18): it only grants its listed 5 points if you successfully fulfilled its requirement during the game (you will see a green check on it). Options Bonanza Module : On : add 4 hidden tiles in the market corners at the beginning of Day/Night phases Off Planned Expansion Variant : On : you have a fixed number of contracts before establishing new outposts (based on your progression on that action) Off : you draw 2 cards to gain contracts before establishing new outposts Automaton (only with Solo) : Level 1 : Automaton starts with 5*1 + 3*2+1*5 coins cards Level 2 : Automaton starts with 4*1 + 3*2+2*5 coins cards Level 3 : Automaton starts with 2*1 + 3*2+2*5+1*10 coins cards random : level is randomly chosen at start between possible levels Player Preferences Interface setting : Zoom icons (+)/(-)/Reset on the top right corner Reset : will make game elements the same size as designed by developer to fit a standard screen (1920px) => common board on the left, player board on the middle, opponent board on the right. If your screen is smaller, you have to scroll down for opponent boards. If your screen is smaller, you have to scroll down for all players. (+) : zoom in to have less elements fit in the screen (-) : zoom out to have more elements fit in the screen Ask for turn confirmation : Enabled/Disabled Default: Enabled If enabled, add a step to click "Confirm" or "Undo"/"Restart" before turn ends Undo buttons style: "Text"/"Icon" Default : Icon If set to "Icon", display 1 arrow icon instead of "Undo last step" and 2 arrow icons instead of "restart turn" Background : Enabled/Disabled Default : Enabled If Enabled, display a light theme background behind game components Player panel details : Enabled/Disabled Default : Enabled If Enabled, display 2 more lines of informations in player side panels : count of each good types + count of each card symbol type in hand Hand of cards : Bottom of window (default) : display hand cards attached to the bottom of the window, in order to continue to view it when scrolling the page Top of game area : displayed on top (= after status bar title and before main board) Near player board : displayed after your own board and limited to its width Display Discard in Hand at anytime Disabled (default): you can only click your cards when you can play them or discard them after action Explore Enabled : you can only click your cards during your actions turn in order to discard at anytime (in order to respect rules and permit edge cases strategies on deck/discard pile)

---

community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] Long game that has almost too much to do. The strategic horizon can be very limited and paths to victory are hard to plot. Extra actions are a necessity in order to progress, so they become the touchstone and I would bet that there is a clear correlation of players with more actions receiving higher scores. It seems like such a general and unforgiving necessity that to lose out on gaining extra actions leaves a player with limited options. Also, it is *very* difficult to figure out who to bid against because it is hard to determine who is leading.

[Rating: 1/10] I am aware that I am against the overwhelming majority here. But this game is not only WAY too abstract for my taste, it also lacks (almost) any means of interaction, with the exception of that awfully awkward auction. Furthermore I fail to see how the game-mechanics are related to what the game is supposed to simulate. This is a game about game mechanics, not about building a colonial enterprise. Thus, if you like abstract games with low interaction and pointracing, this will be your game. Otherwise, if you prefer sophisticated simulations with a high amount of flavour and interaction: Beware

[Rating: 1/10] Interesting bidding mechanics.  Decent game, but the theme just doesn't do it for me.  Seems to take much longer than it should.

[Rating: 1.5/10] 2 solo plays  I expected a MPS core with an added auction, but it was even a little bit less interactive than expected. And rigid. Firstly the once around auction is too controlled and I just don't see a reason behind its logic. The engine building part is also fairly static: just tick the boxes (a.k.a. tech three). It falls somewhere in a similar feel as hansa Teitonica, and yet that one is less balanced, a bit more interactive and hence a tad more interesting.   Better than worker placements though.  The theme, ehm, what theme, is there a theme? The spice bags pieces are cute and that's it.

[Rating: 2/10] mmm... you play a solo game with friends. the worst part is that I've not seen the spirit. You can call it Goa or Minsk or Math4Dummy.

[Rating: 2/10] I've just not been all that impressed after a few plays.  Just seems that there are better options out there to play than this.  I can't stand the once around the table auction.  If you are unlucky enough to be put to the right of the guy that always bids 1 over you, might as well not play.  Well, according to the ratings "2 extremely annoying game won't play this ever again" is accurate for me.  I've passed up many chances to play this because I can't stand it.
